subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]
passage:
Anirban: Wait, don't start! Listen. Rule one, the ball can't touch the drain. Rule two, you may only hop on the left leg. Rule three, if the ball hits the wall twice...
Yamini: How many rules are there?
Anirban: Twenty. I wrote them all. Rule four...
Tanmay: I forgot rule two already.
Yamini: Me too. My legs are getting stiff standing here.
Anirban: But you need to know them!
Tanmay: I'm going to play kho-kho with the others.
Yamini: Sorry, Anirban, it's too much.
Anirban stood in the colony courtyard holding two pages of rules, and the ball rolled quietly away.

qa.q: How many rules did Anirban write?
What was Anirban probably feeling as the others walked away?
qa.a: Anirban was likely hurt and frustrated, standing alone with the pages after all the effort of writing so many rules.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anirban use, and why might it work?
qa.a: Anirban could start with three simple rules, play a round, and add rules only when a problem shows up. Friends can remember a few rules, and playing keeps them interested.

qa.q: How do Yamini and Tanmay see the rule list?
qa.a: Yamini and Tanmay find it too long to remember and tiring to stand through, so to them the list stopped the fun instead of protecting it.

grounding: Anirban prepares a long list of rules before anyone plays, and the others lose interest, forget the rules and leave.
